text: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD) is a global semiconductor company that primarily offers server microprocessors (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs), data processing units (DPUs), Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), and Adaptive System-on-Chip (SoC) products for data centers; CPUs, accelerated processing units (APUs) that integrate CPUs and GPUs, and chipsets for desktop and notebook personal computers; discrete GPUs, and semi-custom SoC products and development services; and embedded CPUs, GPUs, APUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoC products. From time to time, AMD may also sell or license portions of its intellectual property (IP) portfolio. AMD was incorporated under the laws of Delaware on May 1, 1969, and became a publicly held company in 1972. Its common stock is listed on The NASDAQ Global Select Market (NASDAQ) under the symbol “AMD.” The company’s mailing and executive offices are located at 2485 Augustine Drive, Santa Clara, California 95054, and its telephone number is (408) 749-4000. AMD uses a 52- or 53-week fiscal year ending on the last Saturday in December. References to 2022, 2021, and 2020 refer to the fiscal year unless otherwise stated. The company’s trademarks include AMD, AMD Arrow, AMD CDNA, AMD Instinct, AMD RDNA, Alveo, Artix, Athlon, CoolRunner, EPYC, FidelityFX, FirePro, FreeSync, Geode, Infinity Fabric, Kinex, Pensando, Radeon, Radeon Instinct, ROCm, Ryzen, Spartan, Threadripper, UltraScale, UltraScale+, V-Cache, Versal, Virtex, Vitis, Vivado, Xilinx, Zynq and combinations thereof. Microsoft, Windows, DirectX and Xbox One are registered or trademarks of Microsoft Corporation; PCIe is a registered trademark of PCI-SIG Corporation; Linux is a registered trademark of Linus Torvalds; PlayStation is a registered trademark or trademark of Sony Interactive Entertainment, Inc.; Arm is a registered trademark of ARM Limited (or its subsidiaries); Vulkan and the Vulkan logo are registered trademarks of Khronos Group Inc.; Steam and the Steam logo are trademarks or registered trademarks of Valve Corporation. Other names are for informational purposes only and may be trademarks of their respective owners. The company’s website, http://ir.amd.com, provides links to its SEC filings, corporate governance documents, and other materials, which are posted as soon as reasonably practical after electronic filing. The SEC website, www.sec.gov, contains reports, proxy and information statements, and other information about issuers that file electronically with the SEC. Copies of these documents can be obtained by writing to Corporate Secretary, AMD, 7171 Southwest Parkway, M/S B100.T, Austin, Texas 78735, or by emailing Corporate.Secretary@amd.com. The information on the company’s website is not incorporated by reference into this report. AMD is a global semiconductor company, with integrated circuits (ICs) being semiconductor devices that consist of many interconnected transistors on a single chip. Since the invention of the transistor in 1948, improvements in IC process and design technologies have led to smaller, more complex, more reliable ICs at a lower cost-per-function. AMD’s strategy focuses on high-performance and adaptive computing technology, software, and product leadership across data center, embedded, client, and gaming markets through five strategic pillars: compute technology leadership, expanding data center leadership, enabling pervasive artificial intelligence (AI), providing software platforms and developer enablement, and designing custom silicon and solutions. The company invests in high-performance CPUs for cloud infrastructure, enterprise, edge, supercomputing, and PCs; high-performance GPUs and software for gaming, compute, AI, and virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR). With the acquisition of Xilinx, Inc. in February 2022, AMD’s product portfolio now includes FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs for data centers and embedded markets. Additionally, with the acquisition of Pensando Systems, Inc. in May 2022, AMD offers high-performance DPUs and next-generation data center solutions. AMD leverages its CPU, GPU, FPGA, and DPU product portfolios to deliver differentiated solutions at both the chip and systems levels, including semi-custom SoCs, Adaptive SoCs, and APUs, as well as PCs, embedded platforms, and servers. The company has a broad technology roadmap targeting AI training and inference across cloud, edge, and intelligent endpoints through its family of CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoCs. AMD develops world-class software platforms, including development tools, compilers, and drivers for its CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs, and works closely with customers to define and develop customized solutions using its high-performance IP and leadership in design and packaging. The company invests in innovative technologies such as its custom-ready chiplet platform and AMD Infinity Architecture to maintain its position as a preferred custom-design silicon provider. AMD’s four reportable segments are: the Data Center segment, which includes server CPUs and GPUs, DPUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoC products for data centers; the Client segment, which includes CPUs, APUs, and chipsets for desktop and notebook personal computers; the Gaming segment, which includes discrete GPUs, semi-custom SoC products, and development services; and the Embedded segment, which includes embedded CPUs, GPUs, APUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoC products. In addition, AMD has an All Other category that is not a reportable segment. The Data Center segment primarily includes server CPUs, GPUs, DPUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoC products, which address computational and visual data processing needs in data centers. Modern data centers require high-performance, energy-efficient, scalable, and adaptable compute engines to meet demand for data storage, access, analysis, and management. Different combinations of CPUs, GPUs, DPUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoCs optimize performance and power for diverse workloads. Server CPUs in the Data Center segment currently include the AMD EPYC™ Series processors—AMD EPYC 9004 Series, AMD EPYC 7003 Series, and AMD EPYC 7002 Series. The 4th Gen AMD EPYC 9004 Series is part of this product line.

The company offers a range of products including server CPUs, GPUs, DPUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoC products, as well as APUs and discrete GPUs, across multiple segments. The Data Center Segment includes server CPUs such as the AMD EPYC™ Series—specifically the AMD EPYC 9004 Series (based on “Zen 4” architecture), AMD EPYC 7003 Series, and AMD EPYC 7002 Series—and features the AMD 3D V-Cache™ technology in its 3rd Gen processors for enhanced performance in technical computing. It also provides FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs, including Virtex™, Kintex™, Zynq™, Zynq MPSoC, and Versal™ products, along with Alveo™ accelerator cards available on major OEM server platforms and cloud providers via FPGA-as-a-Service (FaaS). DPUs, such as the P4 programmable AMD Pensando DPUs, offload network, storage, and security services from CPUs, enabling cloud and enterprise customers to optimize performance with minimal latency, jitter, and power impact, and power the Aruba CX 10000 top-of-rack switch. Data Center GPUs include the AMD Instinct™ MI200 Series, based on 2nd Gen AMD CDNA architecture, designed for AI training and supercomputing, and paired with the AMD ROCm™ open software platform; visual cloud GPUs are part of the Radeon™ PRO V families, supporting remote visualization workloads like Desktop-as-a-Service, Workstation-as-a-Service, and Cloud Gaming. AMD Accelerated Parallel Processing (GPGPU) enables discrete GPUs to accelerate computational tasks beyond traditional CPU processing through cooperative work with the CPU, leveraging heterogeneous computing to provide superior user experiences and equal memory access, queuing, and execution capabilities for GPUs. The Client Segment includes desktop CPUs such as the AMD Ryzen™ and AMD Athlon™ series, with Ryzen 7000 Series based on “Zen 4” architecture delivering leadership performance for gamers and content creators, and Ryzen 5000 Series featuring up to 16 cores and AMD 3D V-Cache technology. Notebook CPUs include mobile Ryzen and Athlon processors with up to 16 “Zen 4” cores in the Ryzen 7000 Series and “Zen 3+” and “Zen 3” architectures in the Ryzen 6000 and 5000 Series. Commercial CPUs include AMD PRO Mobile and AMD PRO desktop processors with Radeon™ graphics, such as Ryzen PRO, Threadripper™ PRO, and Athlon PRO, offering enhanced security, manageability, and platform longevity; the Ryzen PRO 7030 Series Mobile is built on “Zen 3” architecture. Chipsets include X670 and B650 for AM5 platforms supporting PCIe® 5.0, X570, B550, A520, B450, and A320 for AM4, and WRX80 for high-end desktop and workstation platforms. The Gaming Segment features graphics in APUs, GPUs, SoCs, or discrete GPUs, with RDNA™ 3 as the foundation for next-generation PC gaming and RDNA 2 supporting ray tracing, AMD Infinity Cache™, and variable rate shading; these architectures are used in Sony PlayStation® 5, Microsoft® Xbox Series S™ and X™ consoles. Semi-custom products include SoCs for Sony PlayStation5 and Microsoft Xbox Series S and X, and a semi-custom APU for the Steam Deck™ developed with Valve. Discrete desktop and notebook GPUs include Radeon RX 7900 XTX and RX 7900 XT on RDNA 3 architecture with a 5 nm and 6 nm chiplet design, and Radeon RX 6000 series on RDNA2; these support DirectX® 12 Ultimate, Vulkan®, FreeSync™, FreeSync Premium, and FreeSync Premium Pro, and VR. AMD Radeon Software enables remote gaming and features FidelityFX™, including FSR 2.0, which boosts frame rates with minimal performance loss and similar or better image quality than native resolution without dedicated machine learning hardware. Professional GPUs in the Radeon PRO family support CAD, broadcast, animation, and 3D rendering, with the W6000 series using RDNA 2 and Infinity Cache for reduced latency and power consumption. The Embedded Segment includes embedded CPUs, APUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoCs for automotive, industrial, medical, aerospace, defense, communications, networking, security, storage, and thin clients, with requirements for low power, small form factors, 24x7 operation, and support for Linux®, Windows®, and complex applications, including industrial temperature, shock, vibration, and reliability standards. Embedded products include AMD Embedded EPYC CPUs, Ryzen V-Series and R-Series APUs and CPUs, and SoCs, designed for high-performance networking, security, storage, 3D graphics, and 4K multimedia in automotive infotainment. FPGAs include UltraScale+™ (16 nm), UltraScale™ (20 nm), 7 Series (28 nm), and older series, and Adaptive SoCs include Zynq SoC, UltraScale+ MPSoCs, and the industry’s first RFSoC with integrated RF data converters; the Versal portfolio features a heterogeneous compute platform with Scalar, Adaptable, and Intelligent Engines for AI and big data applications. Development boards, kits, and configuration products provide hardware, tools, IP, and reference designs to accelerate domain-specific application development. Legacy FPGA families include Virtex-6, Virtex-5, Virtex-4, Virtex-II Pro, Virtex-II, and original Virtex, and Spartan-6, Spartan-3, Spartan-3E, Spartan-3A, Spartan-IIE, Spartan-II, Spartan XL, and original Spartan; CPLDs include CoolRunner™ and XC9500. Design platforms and services include FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs with adaptable hardware enabling customized architectures, with FPGAs offering reconfigurable hardware, memory, DSP, analog mixed signal, high-speed transceivers, and networking cores, and Adaptive SoCs providing heterogeneous processing for real-time control, analytics, sensor fusion, and acceleration; Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoCs target wireless, radar, and cable access with integrated RF data converters; Versal delivers powerful heterogeneous acceleration for big data and AI applications and can be programmed by software developers, data scientists, and hardware developers using tools, software, libraries, IP, middleware, and frameworks. The company sells its products through a direct sales force and independent distributors and sales representatives in domestic and international markets, with sales arrangements based on customer-provided product forecasts.

AMD delivers powerful heterogeneous acceleration for a wide range of applications in the era of big data and AI through its Versal hardware and software platform, which leverages leading-edge memory and interfacing technologies. This product family is accessible and programmable by software developers, data scientists, and hardware developers, supported by a comprehensive suite of tools, software stacks, libraries, IP, middleware, and frameworks that enable industry-standard design flows. The company offers a Software Development Platform that includes Vivado™ ML Edition for hardware design teams and Vitis™ and Vitis AI unified software platforms for developing and deploying embedded software and AI applications on FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs. AMD sells its products through a direct sales force and independent distributors and sales representatives in domestic and international markets, with sales based on customer forecasts and not typically requiring minimum purchases. Sales are documented via product quotes, purchase orders, sales order acknowledgments, and contractual agreements, which include standard terms on payment, warranties, and indemnities. Products are generally warranted for one year to conform to specifications and be free from defects, with up to three-year limited warranties for certain product types and other negotiated periods. AMD markets its products under the AMD trademark, with product brands including Ryzen, Ryzen PRO, Threadripper, Threadripper PRO, Athlon, Athlon PRO, and PRO A-Series for desktop and notebook PCs; Radeon graphics for consumer graphics, AMD Embedded Radeon for embedded graphics, Radeon PRO for professional graphics, and Radeon Instinct, Radeon PRO V-series, and AMD Instinct accelerators for data center graphics. Chipsets are also marketed under AMD trademarks. The company offers low-power versions of Athlon, Geode, Ryzen, EPYC, R-Series, and G-Series processors as embedded solutions. FPGA product brands include Virtex-6, Virtex-7, Virtex UltraScale+, Kintex-7, Kintex UltraScale, Kintex UltraScale+, Artix-7, Artix UltraScale+, Spartan-6, and Spartan-7. Adaptive SoC product brands include Zynq-7000, Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC, Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoCs, Versal HBM, Versal Premium, Versal Prime, Versal AI Core, Versal AI Edge, Vitis, and Vivado. Compute and network acceleration boards are sold under the Alveo brand. Marketing efforts include direct and co-marketing programs, cooperative advertising, and market development programs where eligible customers receive reimbursement for advertising and marketing related to AMD products or third-party systems integrating them. Microprocessor customers include OEMs, large public cloud providers, ODMs, system integrators, and independent distributors, as well as online and brick-and-mortar retailers; graphics customers include these plus AIBs. Chipset customers are primarily PC OEMs and motherboard manufacturers. FPGA and Adaptive SoC products are sold across diverse markets such as Aerospace and Defense, Test and Measurement, Industrial, Automotive, Consumers, Broadcast, Communication Infrastructure, and Data Center, either directly or through distributors and OEM partners, with a growing network of VARs and ISVs for Alveo products. AMD collaborates closely with customers to define product features, performance, and timing, and employs application engineers to assist in system design, testing, and qualification, improving time-to-market and fostering long-term relationships. Customers may pay non-recurring engineering fees and purchase prices for products developed using AMD’s CPU, GPU, and APU technologies. One customer accounted for 16% of consolidated net revenue for the year ended December 31, 2022, with sales in the Gaming segment; a loss of this customer would have a material adverse effect. OEM partners include multi-nationals, regional accounts, and global/local system integrators targeting commercial and consumer markets, with increasing focus on the VAR channel and global system integrators for enterprise, HPC, and cloud customers. Third-party distributors resell to OEMs, ODMs, and other customers, often maintaining inventory and receiving protection against price reductions and return rights for discontinued products, with some agreements including stock rotation provisions. AIB manufacturers build board-level products using AMD’s component-level graphics and chipset products, with agreements protecting their inventory from price reductions; AMD also sells directly to system integrators (SIs), who operate with short design cycles and use discrete graphics to differentiate products. In the data center segment, AMD competes with Intel on FPGA, Adaptive SoC, CPU, and DPU products and with NVIDIA on CPU, GPU, and DPU products; ARM-based microprocessors and platforms are also emerging. In the client segment, Intel is the primary CPU competitor, with ARM-based designs gaining traction in PCs. In the gaming segment, NVIDIA is the leading discrete graphics competitor, Intel offers embedded graphics and integrated graphics, and Intel has entered the discrete GPU market; smaller competitors may have greater flexibility but less financial capacity for R&D. In the embedded segment, AMD faces competition from Intel, Lattice, Microsemi (acquired by Microchip), Broadcom, Marvell, Analog Devices, Texas Instruments, and NXP, as well as from ASICs and other programmable logic products such as high-density FPGAs, low-cost FPGAs, ASICs with embedded logic, CPLDs, DSP devices, embedded processors, multi-gigabit transceivers, discrete GPUs, and emerging programmable logic products. Research and development focuses on next-generation processors (CPU and GPU), FPGAs, Adaptive SoCs, accelerators, SOMs, SmartNICs, and associated software, emphasizing improved performance and performance-per-watt in advanced manufacturing processes, logic and interface IP, advanced packaging, and heterogeneous integration. Software development includes design automation tools, optimized software, and libraries for hardware, embedded software, and AI. AMD collaborates with industry leaders and participates in open-source software initiatives across various technologies, with R&D teams located globally, primarily in the U.S. and other countries. Wafers for HPC, FPGA, and Adaptive SoC products are produced via foundry arrangements with TSMC, a Wafer Supply Agreement with GLOBALFOUNDRIES for 12 nm and 14 nm HPC wafers, and purchases from UMC and Samsung. Board-level graphics manufacturing is outsourced to third parties. Assembly, test, mark, and packaging (ATMP) are performed by partners in the Asia-Pacific region, including joint ventures with Tongfu Microelectronics, SPIL, and KYEC. AMD protects its technologies through contracts and intellectual property rights, including copyrights, patents, patent applications, trademarks, trade secrets, and mask work rights. As of December 31, 2022, it held approximately 8,200 U.S. patents and 2,200 pending U.S. applications, totaling about 19,800 worldwide patent matters (13,200 issued, 6,600 pending), with future filings expected. AMD has cross-licensing and technology exchange agreements with other companies and has acquired licenses for technologies used in IP cores and devices, as well as proprietary and open-source software such as compilers for design tools. Sales are primarily based on purchase orders or long-term agreements, which may not reflect actual future sales due to revisions or cancellations; semi-custom SoC orders result in meaningful backlog. Operating results show seasonal variation, with net revenue historically higher in the second half of the year. As of December 31, 2022, AMD had approximately 25,000 employees globally. The company’s mission is to build great products that accelerate next-generation computing experiences, driven by a culture of innovation, diverse perspectives, and engagement. Annual employee surveys show high scores in culture, engagement, and manager quality, with results recognized as among the best in the technology industry. AMD promotes diversity, belonging, and inclusion, with Employee Resource Groups supporting engagement; it was recognized for the sixth consecutive year as a Best Place to Work for LGBTQ+ equality by the Human Rights Campaign Foundation and included in Bloomberg’s Gender Equality Index for four consecutive years. The company focuses on hiring and developing underrepresented groups and women leaders, with Dr. Lisa Su, CEO, recognized in 2022 as among “Fortune’s Most Powerful Women,” receiving the “Woman Innovation Award” from the Global Semiconductor Alliance, and being listed in Barron’s and Forbes’ top CEO lists. Total rewards include competitive salaries, incentives, and benefits aligned with employee preferences and market conditions, with a strong performance-based culture and strong short-term and long-term incentives, enabling the attraction and retention of approximately 10,000 new employees through acquisitions and direct hiring in fiscal year 2022. Development opportunities are available for career advancement, with most new leaders promoted from within.

Dr. Lisa Su is recognized for her business and leadership achievements. In 2022, she was included in “Fortune’s Most Powerful Women.” Over the past two years, she has received the “Woman Innovation Award” from the Global Semiconductor Alliance and has been listed among Barron’s World’s Best CEOs and Forbes’ World’s Most Powerful Women. She also continues to support President Biden’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. The company invests in its workforce by offering competitive salaries, incentives, and benefits tailored to employee preferences and market conditions, fostering a strong pay-for-performance culture. Employees have benefited from robust financial results, including strong short-term and long-term incentives. These rewards programs have helped attract, retain, and motivate employees, including approximately 10,000 new hires added through acquisitions and direct hiring during fiscal year 2022. Employees are given opportunities to advance their careers, with the majority of new leaders promoted from within. The company emphasizes leadership progression and offers highly rated manager and leadership development programs, along with specialized development initiatives. Operations and properties are subject to U.S. and foreign environmental laws and regulations covering materials used in products, manufacturing processes, pollutant discharges, waste treatment, transport, storage, disposal, and remediation. Suppliers must obtain permits for operations involving air pollutants and wastewater. Environmental laws are complex, frequently change, and have become more stringent, with the European Union and China implementing restrictions on lead and other materials in electronic products. Jurisdictions such as the EU, Australia, California, and China are developing or have implemented market entry or public procurement regulations based on ENERGY STAR specifications and energy consumption limits. Certain laws, including the U.S. Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (Superfund Act), impose strict or joint and several liability on current and prior owners or operators of real property for hazardous substance removal or remediation, even if they were unaware of or not responsible for releases. These laws also hold persons who arrange for hazardous substances to be sent to disposal or treatment facilities liable if those facilities are found contaminated, regardless of ownership. AMD has been named a responsible party on Superfund clean-up orders for three sites in Sunnyvale, California, on the National Priorities List. Since 1981, hazardous material releases to groundwater from former underground tanks have been discovered and remediation efforts have been initiated. In 1991, the California Regional Water Quality Control Board issued Final Site Clean-up Requirements Orders for these sites. Settlement agreements with other responsible parties have been reached for two of the orders, with those parties agreeing to assume most foreseeable costs and lead remediation activities. AMD remains responsible for additional costs beyond the agreements and for all remaining costs if other parties fail to fulfill their obligations. To address future remediation costs, an estimated environmental liability of approximately $3.9 million has been recorded, with no potential insurance recoveries included. The progress of future remediation efforts cannot be predicted with certainty, and costs may change; however, the company believes any additional costs beyond the accrued amount would not be material. Key risks include Intel Corporation’s dominance in the microprocessor market and its aggressive business practices, which may limit AMD’s ability to compete on a level playing field. Intel’s market share, margins, and financial resources allow it to market aggressively, target customers and channel partners, and influence customer decisions. Intel controls x86 microprocessor and computer system standards, benchmarks, and platform components, including core logic chipsets, graphics chips, networking devices, and non-volatile storage, and has established de facto standards that can delay access for other companies. Intel’s influence over PC manufacturers, motherboard suppliers, memory providers, BIOS developers, and software companies, along with its marketing and advertising efforts, can negatively impact AMD’s sales and margins. Intel’s greater financial resources and investments in marketing, research and development, and new manufacturing facilities, as well as its use of advanced process technologies and early product introductions, increase AMD’s vulnerability. Intel may also disadvantage AMD’s discrete graphics processing units (GPUs) by granting preferential access to its proprietary graphics interface or restricting access to external companies, and by releasing its own high-end gaming-focused GPUs. AMD also competes with Intel in field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and Adaptive SoC products. Global economic and market uncertainty may negatively impact AMD’s business, as weak PC market conditions and inventory corrections in the second half of 2022 reduced Client segment revenue. Uncertain economic conditions, such as inflation, interest rates, or recession, can reduce consumer confidence and spending, leading customers to delay or cancel purchases. A small number of customers account for a substantial portion of AMD’s revenue, increasing the risk of payment defaults. Customer financial difficulties or insolvency could impair payment of accounts receivable, affecting earnings and cash flow. Key suppliers may also reduce output or become insolvent, disrupting product manufacturing. Economic uncertainty may also hinder the company’s ability to raise capital through debt or equity sales. The semiconductor industry is highly cyclical and has experienced severe downturns that have materially adversely affected AMD’s business in the past and may continue to do so. These downturns are driven by rapid technological change, supply and demand fluctuations, price erosion, and declines in end-user demand, such as for PCs. AMD’s financial performance has been negatively impacted by these downturns, particularly in the second half of 2022 due to weak PC market conditions. Growth depends on demand from emerging global markets, which requires establishing local infrastructure and relationships. If demand in these markets falls short of expectations, sales could decline. Demand for AMD’s products also depends on market conditions in the industries that use them; fluctuations or declines in these markets could materially harm results of operations. Client segment revenue is concentrated in consumer desktop and notebook PCs, which declined in the second half of 2022 due to weak macroeconomic conditions and inventory corrections. Past declines in Client and Gaming segments have been driven by smaller form factors, increased competition, and changes in replacement cycles. The success of semi-custom SoC products depends on securing customers for the design pipeline and favorable consumer market conditions, including the performance of Sony PlayStation® 5, Microsoft® XboxTM Series S and Series X consoles, and next-generation consoles for Sony and Microsoft. The GPU market has seen elevated demand due to cryptocurrency mining, which has affected AMD’s GPU revenue. Demand for cryptocurrency has been volatile, with China banning mining activities and the emergence of new national cryptocurrencies, leading to significant fluctuations in mining interest. If AMD cannot manage these risks, it could face adverse impacts.

2022 saw a decline in revenues due to weak macroeconomic conditions in the PC market and inventory correction actions across the PC supply chain. Revenues from the Client and Gaming segments declined due to factors such as the adoption of smaller and alternative form factors, increased competition, and changes in replacement cycles. The success of semi-custom SoC products depends on securing customers for the semi-custom design pipeline and favorable consumer market conditions, including the performance of the Sony PlayStation® 5, Microsoft® XboxTM Series S, Microsoft® XboxTM Series X, and next-generation consoles for Sony and Microsoft globally. The GPU market has experienced elevated demand due to cryptocurrency mining, with GPU revenue affected by the volatility of that market; demand for cryptocurrency has changed and is expected to continue changing quickly, including due to China’s ban on mining activities and the emergence of new national cryptocurrencies, which could cause significant fluctuations. If the company cannot manage the volatility of the cryptocurrency mining market, its GPU business could be materially harmed. The loss of a major customer could materially harm the business, as a small number of customers currently account for a substantial portion of revenue and are expected to continue doing so; a reduction or cessation of purchases by a key customer would materially adversely affect operations. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic could materially harm the business, financial condition, and results of operations due to public health measures such as quarantines, business closures, travel bans, and restrictions on gatherings and mobility, which are frequently updated with little notice and continue to disrupt operations. Even as employees return to offices, safety efforts may not succeed, and employees may face health risks or be unable to work efficiently from home, leading to delays in product schedules, missed customer commitments, and reduced productivity. The pandemic has also disrupted global supply chains, affecting service providers, logistics, and the availability of supplies and products. The company has taken steps to maintain stable material supply through long-term purchase commitments and prepayments with suppliers, but if stable procurement of equipment, materials, or substrates at reasonable costs cannot be maintained, it could materially harm the business. Product schedules and roadmaps may be adjusted to support remote work and shifting market demands, and delays, reductions, or cancellations in product supply due to facility closures, border restrictions, transportation delays, labor shortages, or workforce mobility limitations by third-party manufacturers, back-end manufacturers, warehouses, partners, or vendors could materially harm operations. The pandemic has also negatively impacted the global economy, reducing consumer confidence and spending, which may lead to delayed or canceled purchases or payment defaults, and even in periods of strong demand, long-term sustainability remains uncertain due to economic volatility. The pandemic has also caused disruptions in global capital and financial markets; although the company believes its cash, cash equivalents, short-term investments, Revolving Credit Agreement, and operating cash flows will cover operations and commitments for the next 12 months and beyond, additional funding may not be available due to market conditions, which could adversely affect the business. The extent of the pandemic’s impact depends on unpredictable and highly uncertain factors such as the spread, duration, and severity of the virus, new variants, business disruptions, availability of treatments and vaccines, and public health measures. The markets in which the company sells its products are highly competitive, with product competitiveness determined by timely introductions, quality, features, energy efficiency, reliability, performance, form factor, price, cost, adherence to standards, integration, software compatibility, ease of use, functionality, security, and brand recognition. Competition is expected to remain intense due to rapid technological changes, frequent product launches by competitors, new entrants offering better performance or features, aggressive pricing, and competitors’ strong marketing and sales resources. Competitors may have greater access to complementary technologies, such as interface, processor, and memory information; for instance, improvements in integrated graphics may reduce demand for discrete graphics chips. If competitors launch new products before the company, demand for its products could decline. Intel’s expansion into integrated graphics for high-end discrete solutions across computing segments may negatively impact its competitiveness, and competition from ARM-based designs could grow the ARM ecosystem. The company faces competition from new entrants who may adapt more quickly to customer needs and emerging technologies, and some customers may develop similar products internally. The company may face delays in R&D or be required to invest more than expected, and industry consolidation could reduce the number of suppliers, customers, and partners, adversely affecting the business. Operating results are subject to quarterly and seasonal sales patterns, with a large portion of sales historically occurring in the final month of each quarter, making revenue forecasting difficult and increasing the risk of unanticipated variations. Seasonal trends typically show higher net revenue in the second half of the year, though market conditions and product transitions may alter this. Many of these trends are beyond the company’s control. If the company cannot adequately protect its technology or intellectual property through patents, copyrights, trade secrets, trademarks, or other measures, it may lose a competitive advantage and incur significant expenses. The company relies on contracts, confidentiality agreements, copyrights, patents, trademarks, and common law rights like trade secrets to protect its intellectual property, but cannot guarantee protection from infringement or misappropriation in the U.S. or abroad. Patents may be challenged, invalidated, expire, or be circumvented, and patent applications may not result in issued patents or may not provide a competitive advantage. Others may independently develop similar products, duplicate offerings, or design around patents, and enforcement of intellectual property is difficult and costly globally, especially in jurisdictions with weaker protections, which could materially harm the business. Unfavorable currency exchange rate fluctuations could adversely affect the company, as costs, assets, and liabilities are denominated in foreign currencies, increasing foreign-denominated expenses as a percentage of revenue and affecting profitability and cash flows. The company hedges a portion of its foreign currency exposure using projections of long-term expenditures such as payroll, but cannot guarantee effectiveness; failure to hedge could harm financial performance. Additionally, most product sales are in U.S. dollars, so an appreciation of the U.S. dollar relative to local currencies could reduce product sales in those markets. The company relies on third parties to manufacture its products, including TSMC for microprocessor and GPU wafers at 7 nm or smaller nodes and GLOBALFOUNDRIES (GF) for larger nodes, and UMC and Samsung for programmable logic devices. It also relies on third-party manufacturers for assembly, testing, marking, and packaging (ATMP). The company has no long-term contracts with some suppliers and depends on them to allocate capacity, maintain quality, yield, and timely delivery at acceptable prices. These manufacturers also serve competitors and may prioritize other customers, increase prices, require prepayments, or reduce deliveries, which could materially harm the business. Risks include limited control over delivery schedules, yield, cycle times, quality, pricing, capacity during high demand, intellectual property misappropriation, dependence on subcontractors, and limited inventory management. Disruptions such as facility damage, financial difficulties, power outages, lack of raw materials, or political and economic instability in suppliers could cause supply delays. Transitioning production to new manufacturers may result in delayed introductions, lower yields, or poor performance. If product quality issues arise or capacity is lost, the company may be unable to secure timely alternative supply, leading to significant shipment delays. The company has a wafer supply agreement (WSA) with GF through 2025, amended in May 2021 and December 2021, which includes a minimum annual capacity allocation and corresponding wafer purchase targets; failure to meet targets requires payment of the difference. AMD is obligated to pre-pay GF for wafers in 2022 and 2023. The amended agreement removes exclusivity and allows full flexibility to contract with any foundry at any node. If actual wafer needs are below the target, excess inventory or higher unit costs could reduce gross margins. If GF fails to meet its capacity allocation, product shipment delays could occur. The company is also party to two ATMP joint ventures with affiliates of Tongfu Microelectronics Co., Ltd., which provide the majority of ATMP services, but there is no guarantee they will meet long-term requirements; delays or supply issues from these joint ventures could result in lost sales. If essential equipment, materials, substrates, or manufacturing processes are unavailable, the company could be materially adversely affected. The company purchases equipment, materials, and substrates from multiple suppliers and depends on timely deliveries to its back-end manufacturing service providers.

For the year ended December 31, 2022, the company repurchased 36,326,137 shares, with average prices per share of $121.03, $90.58, $89.52, and $71.75 during the respective quarters, and the total maximum dollar value that may yet be purchased under the program was $36,326,137.

During the fiscal year 2022, Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD) returned a total of $3.7 billion to shareholders through the repurchase of 36.3 million shares of common stock under its stock repurchase program. The repurchases occurred in specific periods: from March 27, 2022, to June 25, 2022, 10,159,900 shares were repurchased at an average price of $90.58, totaling $7,407 million; from June 26, 2022, to September 24, 2022, 6,895,972 shares were repurchased at an average price of $89.52, totaling $6,790 million; from September 25, 2022, to December 31, 2022, 3,484,459 shares were repurchased at an average price of $71.75, totaling $6,540 million. Additional repurchases took place during the last fiscal quarter of 2022: from September 25, 2022, to October 29, 2022, no shares were repurchased; from October 30, 2022, to November 26, 2022, 1,455,994 shares were repurchased at an average price of $70.65, totaling $6,687 million; and from November 27, 2022, to December 31, 2022, 2,028,465 shares were repurchased at an average price of $72.54, totaling $6,540 million. The total shares repurchased during the year were 3,484,459. Shares withheld as payment of withholding taxes in connection with the vesting or exercise of equity awards are treated as common stock repurchases, but are not considered repurchases under an authorized common stock repurchase plan. During fiscal year 2022, AMD withheld 5 million shares for such purposes. Net revenue for 2022 was $23.6 billion, a 44% increase from $16.4 billion in 2021, driven by a 64% increase in Data Center segment revenue due to higher sales of EPYC™ server processors, a 21% increase in Gaming segment revenue from higher semi-custom product sales, and a significant increase in Embedded segment revenue from the inclusion of Xilinx embedded product sales. This growth was partially offset by a 10% decrease in Client segment revenue due to lower processor shipments from a weak PC market and inventory correction actions. Gross margin for 2022 was 45%, down from 48% in 2021, primarily due to amortization of intangible assets from the Xilinx acquisition. Operating income for 2022 was $1.3 billion, compared to $3.6 billion in 2021, and net income was $1.3 billion, down from $3.2 billion in the prior year, both primarily due to lower operating income. Cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments as of December 31, 2022, were $5.9 billion, compared to $3.6 billion at the end of 2021. Total debt as of December 31, 2022, was $2.5 billion, up from $313 million at December 25, 2021. In June 2022, AMD issued $1.0 billion in senior notes: $500 million of 3.924% Senior Notes due 2032 and $500 million of 4.393% Senior Notes due 2052, both senior unsecured obligations. In the same month, AMD entered into a five-year unsecured revolving credit facility of $3.0 billion, with no funds drawn during the year. In November 2022, AMD established a commercial paper program allowing issuance of unsecured commercial paper notes up to a maximum principal amount of $3.0 billion with a maturity of up to 397 days, but as of December 31, 2022, no commercial paper was outstanding. As of December 31, 2022, $6.5 billion remained available for future stock repurchases under the program, which is not obligated to acquire shares, has no termination date, and may be suspended or discontinued at any time. In February 2022, AMD completed the acquisition of Xilinx, Inc., expanding its product portfolio to include Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), Adaptive SoCs, and Adaptive Compute Acceleration Platform (ACAP) products, and entering multiple embedded markets. In May 2022, AMD acquired Pensando Systems, Inc., enhancing its data center solutions with high-performance data processing units (DPUs) and a complementary software stack. These acquisitions positioned AMD to offer the industry’s broadest set of leadership compute engines and accelerators. In 2022, AMD launched several new products, including 4th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors with next-generation architecture, 3rd Gen EPYC processors with AMD 3D V-Cache technology, the 7 nm Versal™ ACAP VCK5000 development card, the AMD Instinct™ MI210 accelerator, and ROCm™ 5 software. In the Embedded segment, AMD introduced the Ryzen™ Embedded R2000 Series and the Kria™ KR260 Robotics Starter Kit. In the Client segment, AMD launched the Ryzen 7000 Series Desktop and Mobile processors powered by the “Zen 4” architecture, the Ryzen 6000 Series Mobile processors with “Zen 3+” architecture and integrated graphics, the Ryzen 5000 C-Series processors for premium Chrome OS devices, and the Ryzen Threadripper™ PRO 5000 WX-Series and Ryzen PRO 7030 Series Mobile processors. In the Gaming segment, AMD unveiled the Radeon™ RX 7900 XTX and RX 7900 XT graphics cards based on the next-generation RDNA™ 3 architecture, new RX 6950 XT, RX 6750 XT, and RX 6650 XT cards based on RDNA 2 with GDDR6 memory at up to 18Gbps, and the Radeon PRO W6400 GPU. Revenue allowances are determined under ASC 606-10-32-8 through 14 by estimating the most likely amount of consideration after adjusting for rights of return, rebates to OEM customers, and price protection or rebates to distributor customers, based on historical activity, known events, and current economic conditions. Adjustments for distributor price incentives and price protection are based on historical incentives and known future price movements, while OEM rebate estimates use historical rebate attainment rates and market data analysis. For cooperative advertising and marketing promotions, reductions to revenue are recognized when the related revenue is recognized if the funds can be estimated; otherwise, they are recognized at the later of when the revenue transaction occurs or when the program is offered.
